Russell Investments — Campus Recruitment Experience 
 
 
 
 
 
Summer Internship Interview Experience 
Stipend: 60,000/month 
 
 
 
Anya Agrawal 
Electrical Engineering

Russell Investments came to campus just after Diwali for 2 roles — Asset Allocation and Risk 
Investment. The OAs for both were held together on 5th November on campus. Out of all the 
students that had applied, 60 were selected for each role to sit for the OA. 
 
Online Assessment (OA) 
The OA was the same for both roles — 22 questions with a time limit of 1 hour. 20 were MCQs 
and 2 were coding questions, they were not separated into distinct sections. You need to keep 
a close eye on the timer while solving the MCQs so you leave adequate time for the coding 
questions. 
 
MCQ Breakdown 
The MCQs fell broadly into three categories: 
• Code Snippets: These were relatively straightforward — pseudo code was given and you 
either had to complete the code or identify possible outputs. 
• Financial Maths: Compound interest, pattern finding, rate of return, P/E ratio, and some 
probability questions. 
• Financial Knowledge: Portfolio risk assessment, hypothesis testing, covariance testing, 
and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF). 
 
Coding Questions 
The 2 coding questions were relatively manageable: 
• Candy distribution problem: Two siblings (older sister and younger brother) had to be 
given candies such that the sister always got more than the brother, based on the 
formula k×(a+x) = b×y, where a = candies to sister, b = candies to brother, and (x + y) = 
minimum total candies. 
• Stock market max profit: Find the day where the stock earned maximum profit. I didn't 
get time to attempt this one, but something similar is available on LeetCode — worth a 
look. 
 
Results 
OA results were declared on the same day at 9:30 PM, with interviews scheduled for 10 AM the 
next morning. Yes, it was quite a short window to prepare. 20 were shortlisted for Asset 
Allocation and 17 for Risk Investment.

Pre-Placement Talk 
Before the interviews began, there was a pre-placement talk where they told us all about the 
company and the heads of the respective roles came up to explain what each role covered, 
followed by a Q&A session. There were 2 panels for each role. Don't skip this — firstly because 
this sets an expectation for what they expect out of you and secondly this gives you an 
opportunity to ask questions to the company as a whole – the right question can give you the 
edge so chose your questions wisely, my advise would be to centre them around the current 
affairs. 
 
Interview Round 1 
This was my first interview ever, and I was first on the list — so naturally the anxiety was 
through the roof. My panel had just one interviewer, and I think he sensed the nerves and 
actively tried to ease the environment before we got started. The round lasted around 30 
minutes and was largely conversational. Here's roughly how it went: 
 
• Why this role? — What attracted you to Asset Allocation / Risk Investment. 
• Resume walkthrough — He went through my resume and asked me to explain my main 
project and give a demo. 
• Financial concepts — Terms like the Sharpe ratio came up.  
• OA reflection — He asked which questions I liked in the OA. 
• HR questions — Strengths, weaknesses, the usual. 
• Puzzle at the end — 100 hens sitting in a circle. Each hen will peck at least once, either 
the hen to its right or left. Find the maximum number of hens that remain unpecked. 
 
The Hen Puzzle — Solution 
A hen remains unpecked only when both neighbours peck away from it. So think in groups of 3 
— the unpecked hen sits in the middle with the two on either side pecking outward. 100 ÷ 3 = 
33. I didn't get it immediately, and the interviewer did help me through it — don't be afraid to 
think out loud and ask help. 
 
One important thing to note was that the interview was actually built around my OA 
performance; they had a full analysis showing strengths and weaknesses, and my maths and 
financials clearly outshone my coding which shaped the direction of questions.

Interview Round 2 
6 out of 20 made it through to Round 2, which had a full panel of 3 interviewers. One advantage 
here — I wasn't first in line, so I had time to ask others who'd already been in and what it was 
like.  
The round covered three distinct parts: 
 
1. Personal Interest & Beyond the Resume 
They asked about something that wasn't on my resume and about my personal interests. I 
spoke about finance and wrapped it up by mentioning my interest in motorsport — I put a 
genuine opinion out there, and I think that authenticity worked in my favour.  
 
2. Finance Case Question 
This was the hardest part. They presented different individuals with varying backgrounds and 
asked me to classify how each would invest across three categories — equities, savings, and 
bonds. I honestly had very little idea. I gave an answer based on whatever I knew, I'm fairly sure 
it was wrong, and I'm fairly sure the panel knew that too. I thought it was over for me — but we 
continued. This is the time where complete panic takes over you. It is very important that you 
keep calm, the interviewers do help you out and want you to excel. They want to test how you 
would do in such situations.  
 
3. Puzzle Round 
Simple logic-based puzzles came next — things I was already somewhat aware of because I'd 
spoken to peers who went before me. I'd highly recommend watching TED-Ed or TED Talk 
videos on classic logic puzzles before your interview. The Infinity Hotel problem and various 
sorting problems are fair game.  
 
The Closing Question 
The interview closed with a question I genuinely didn't expect: “What makes you the happiest 
in your life?” That one still gets me thinking. There's no right answer to this — just be honest. 
 
Final Outcome 
Then came the stressful waiting time — and then the announcement on the spot. Quite a 
relieving moment.

Key Takeaways  
 
Preparation 
For the OA, don't just focus on one area — cover everything. On the coding side, Striver's A2Z 
sheet and LeetCode are your best friends. For those from non-CS/IT branches who feel coding 
isn't their strongest suit, don't let that discourage you. Keep your maths and logic sharp 
because a strong performance there can carry you through the OA even if you might think that 
you have bombed the coding. Beyond the OA itself, take some time to read about the company 
and understand what the roles actually involve. This would also help you out in the OA 
 
Time Management 
This goes beyond just pacing yourself in the OA. Be early — not on time, early. Carry a pen and 
a notebook to every stage of the process, from the pre-placement talk through to your 
interviews. Jotting things down during the pre-placement talk helps you pick up useful details 
that can feed directly into your interview answers. In the interview itself, using a notebook to 
work through a problem lets the interviewer see how you think, not just what you conclude — 
and that visibility into your process can make a real difference. 
 
Communication 
I can’t emphasize enough about this one. Judge the scenario of the interview and go with the 
flow – don’t restrict yourself to a question-and-answer vibe. And also be open to small talk – 
this helps them gauge your personality. One thing that genuinely makes a difference is thinking 
out loud. Don't rush straight to an answer — interviewers want to follow your reasoning. This 
matters even more when you're wrong. And before you even walk into the room, spend 10 
minutes talking to whoever came out before you. Once you're in there, be upfront about where 
you're strong and where you're stuck as they will genuinely try to help you out. 
 
Be Yourself 
It sounds obvious, but don't script yourself. The moment you start reciting a rehearsed answer, 
the panel can tell — and it closes you off from the moments that actually land. Let your real 
interests come through, even the unexpected ones. In my Round 2, mentioning motorsport 
genuinely seemed to work in my favour — not because it was impressive, but because it was 
real. By the second round especially, they're not just assessing whether you can answer 
questions. They want to know if they'd enjoy working with you. So show up as yourself, not as 
who you think they want to see. 
 
Feel free to reach out if you have any doubts – on my mail, LinkedIn or in campus :)
